PMID: 25451608
Title: Negative affectivity predicts decreased pain tolerance during low-grade inflammation in healthy women.
Source: Brain, behavior, and immunity (2015)
Abstract: INTRODUCTION: Experimental animal studies provided evidence for a synergistic effect of immunological and psychological stressors on subsequent sickness behaviours. Up to now, little corroborating evidence for such synergy exists for humans, in whom it may provide a mechanism leading to the expression of functional somatic symptoms. The aim of the present study was to determine an interaction between stress(-vulnerability) and an immunological activation on experimental pain sensitivity, i.e., pressure pain threshold and tolerance in healthy humans. METHODS: In healthy female participants (n=25, mean age 22.3 years), negative affectivity (NA) and experienced stress were assessed by questionnaire before receiving a Salmonella typhi vaccine or saline control in a randomized blinded cross-over design. Pressure pain threshold was assessed at the lower back and calves and pain tolerance was assessed at the thumbnail, before and six hours after each injection. RESULTS: Vaccination induced leukocytosis (+100%) and increased serum IL-6 (+670%). NA predicted decreased pain tolerance after vaccination (β=-.57, p=.007), but not after placebo (β=.25, p=.26). key_findings.finding: One directly qualifying study was identified: PMID 25451608, “Negative affectivity predicts decreased pain tolerance during low-grade inflammation in healthy women.” It enrolled 25 healthy women (mean age 22.3 years) in a randomized, blinded, saline-controlled crossover study; inflammation was induced with Salmonella typhi vaccine, which produced leukocytosis (+100%) and IL-6 (+670%). Pressure pain thresholds were measured at the lower back and calves, and thumbnail pain tolerance was measured before and 6 hours after injection. Baseline negative affectivity predicted reduced post-vaccination pain tolerance (β = −0.57, p = .007), but not placebo-session tolerance (β = .25, p = .26).
